Thank you for the opportunity to provide us an update on, to provide you an update on exciting project that reflects Henrico County Public Schools commitment to innovative learning environments and student success.

Today we're excited to provide an update on the environmental education living building. This project represents much more than a new facility. It is an investment in how students across Henrico experience learning, connected rigorous curriculum with authentic place-based experiences.

The living building will serve as an instructional hub for the Verina Center for Environmental Studies and Sustainability while also creating new learning opportunities for students across the division. This work connects directly to our Journey to 2030 strategic plan, specifically academic achievement and learning environment.

There are four connections I'd like to take a moment to emphasize. The Living Building creates rigorous, meaningful, and authentic learning experiences. It provides opportunities for students to engage in project-based experiential and role-world learning. And that learning will occur in a community-connected infrastructure that creates a welcoming learning space.

And finally, the facility itself demonstrates our commitment to efficient green energy solutions in new construction. Those priorities come together in this project. The facility supports what students are learning, how they are learning it, and the environment in which that learning occurs.
At this time, I will turn the presentation over to Susan Moore, Director of Capital Outlay and Planning. Good afternoon, Chair Irving, Board Members, and Dr. Cashwell.

As a reminder, our living building project is located on a portion of the land formerly known as Wilton Farm, which is an approximate 1,200-acre parcel of forested and agricultural land near Osborne Turnpike and the James River.

The Wilton Farm was established in the 1600s, however, this property has historical roots that run far deeper. The site and surroundings are rich with early Native American history as well as revolutionary and colonial ties. The original home was built in 1753 and the site was visited by notable historic figures, including George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Patrick Henry, Lafayette and his troops, just to name a few. The yellow highlighted area is the approximate 60-acre

site that HCPS is utilizing. The locator symbol shows the location of the new building on a gently sloping open field near Whale Lake. This location is ideal as it is far enough away from the overpass so that vehicular noise isn't audible at the building, nor will it be visible.

Utilizing the clearing means that no trees needed to be removed for the construction of the new building, and the proximity to the lake allows curriculum to include learning modules on wetlands, water quality, native flora and fauna, and other environmental topics. This slide zooms in on our site and is annotated to show the major landscape features. At the top center, a proposed orchard is shown in a circular Fibonacci sequence pattern, which is envisioned as

an opportunity for students to leave their mark on the school in sight. For example, each graduating class is invited to plant a tree to commemorate the time they spent at this site so that this mini forest will grow slowly over time, offering an opportunity to watch the trees life cycles. The site will feature various educational stations which will cover the aspects of nature, the environment, and the history of the site.
